title: Foundations
intro: Three related frameworks, all from Chris Eliasmith's group and collaborators, show how to get from 'a population of spiking neurons' to 'a system that represents, computes, remembers and reasons'. They are the most complete engineering toolkit there is for building cognition out of spikes.

blocks.text: A spiking neural network on its own is a dynamical system with no stated purpose. To make it do something specific, such as hold a value, compute a function, remember the recent past or answer a question, you need a method that maps a description of the job onto connection weights. The pages in this section cover three such methods, each built on the one before.

items: Neural Engineering Framework (NEF): the base layer. A population of neurons represents a vector; connections between populations compute functions of that vector; recurrent connections implement dynamical systems. Weights are solved for, not trained by gradient descent.

Semantic Pointer Architecture (SPA): a cognitive layer on top of the NEF. Concepts are high-dimensional vectors (semantic pointers), combined by binding (circular convolution) and bundling (addition) into structured representations such as 'colour ⊛ RED + shape ⊛ SQUARE'. Spaun, a 2.5-million-neuron model that does eight different tasks, was built this way.

Legendre Memory Unit (LMU): a memory layer. The Legendre Delay Network is a small linear system, derived with NEF-style dynamics, that holds an optimal compressed record of a sliding window of input history. As a recurrent cell it beats LSTMs on several long-memory benchmarks.

blocks.text: Why this matters for a cortical column

The Thousand Brains Theory and HTM describe what a cortical column should do: learn objects as features at locations, predict the next input, vote with neighbouring columns. They say less about how to wire spiking neurons to do it. The NEF supplies that missing step. Once you can write down a quantity a layer of the column should carry, such as a location in an object's reference frame, a movement vector, or a sensed feature, the NEF tells you how many neurons it takes, what their tuning curves look like, and what weights compute the update between layers. Path integration (location ← location + movement) is a textbook NEF integrator. A column's 'object' representation can be a semantic pointer, and voting between columns can be a clean-up memory.

The two traditions also differ in instructive ways. HTM learns with local Hebbian growth of dendritic segments and uses binary sparse codes. The NEF mostly solves for weights offline and uses dense, heterogeneous rate-like codes, though it can learn online with the PES rule. Building a column will likely borrow from both: NEF methods for the continuous quantities (locations, velocities, grid-cell phases), and HTM-style sparse sequence learning for the predictive layer.

items: Start with the NEF page and play with the tuning-curve and decoding widgets until 'population → vector → decoded function' feels concrete.
Then the Semantic Pointers page, for how symbols and structure ride on vectors.
Then the LMU page, for memory of time series, which a column needs to predict sequences.
Then the hardware section, to see where these models can actually run in real time.
